key_terms.meaning: F = N I, the coil ampere-turns that drive flux around a magnetic path; unit ampere-turn (A·t)
S = l/(μ₀μᵣA), opposition of a magnetic path to flux; unit ampere-turn per weber (A/Wb)
A short air length in the iron path; its reluctance is μᵣ times that of the same length of iron, so it controls the total
B = Φ/A, flux per unit area; unit tesla (T)
e = −dλ/dt; a changing flux linkage λ in a coil induces an EMF e
L = λ/I; for a coil on a core, L = N²/S, so more turns or less reluctance give more inductance
M = λ₂/I₁, the flux linkage in coil 2 per ampere in coil 1
k = M/√(L₁L₂), between 0 (no shared flux) and 1 (all flux shared)
a = N₁/N₂ = V₁/V₂; secondary voltage follows the turns count
Core built from thin, insulated steel sheets, so eddy currents cannot flow in large loops
Rated voltage × rated current of a transformer; stated in kVA because losses fix the limit, not the load power factor
E_b = V − I_aR_a, the EMF a spinning motor armature generates against the supply
Segmented ring with brushes that reverses coil connections, acting as a mechanical rectifier in a generator and inverter in a motor
N_s = 120f/P, the speed of the rotating field; f is supply frequency in Hz, P the pole count
s = (N_s − N)/N_s; the rotor runs slightly slower than the field, and rotor frequency is s·f
The highest torque a motor can develop, reached at slip s_max = R₂/X₂; beyond it torque falls again
A pulsating single-phase field split into two equal fields rotating opposite ways; they cancel at standstill, so no starting torque
A series-wound commutator motor with laminated field that runs on either AC or DC, common in mixers and drills
DC field current sets the internal EMF; over-exciting a synchronous motor makes it draw leading current and correct power factor
Degrees the shaft turns per input pulse: 360° ÷ steps per revolution, e.g. 1.8° for a 200-step motor

takeaways: A magnetic circuit obeys the same rule as a resistive one, MMF = flux × reluctance, and one millimetre of air can outweigh a metre of iron.
Inductance is only flux linkage per ampere, so any coil's L is fixed by its turns and the reluctance of its path.
A transformer transfers power by shared flux, not by contact, so volts per turn are equal on both windings and V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁.
A DC machine is one hardware with two behaviours: spin it to generate, feed it to drive, and back EMF is what limits the current it takes.
A three-phase winding alone produces a rotating field; the rotor just chases it, and slip is the small lag that keeps torque flowing.
A single-phase winding gives no starting torque on its own, so every single-phase motor needs a start winding, capacitor or shaded pole.
A synchronous machine locks to supply frequency, which gives exact speed and adjustable power factor but zero self-starting torque.
Special machines are chosen by the control they allow: stepper for open-loop steps, servo for closed-loop position, BLDC for efficient electronic commutation.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on labelled construction sketches, a clean statement and derivation of the governing relation (turns ratio, EMF equation, torque–slip curve), and a short list of real applications for each machine.

bank.q: Define MMF, flux and reluctance. Show that a magnetic circuit is analogous to a resistive circuit, and explain why even a thin air gap can control the flux in an iron core.
outline: F = NI drives flux Φ through reluctance S = l/(μ₀μᵣA)
Compare with EMF, current and resistance; state the analogy line by line
Because μᵣ of iron is in the thousands and of air is 1, a millimetre gap can exceed a metre of iron in reluctance
Consequence: flux is set mainly by gap length; machines are designed with a deliberate gap

bank.q: State Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction. Define self-inductance and mutual inductance and obtain the EMF induced in a coil in terms of its inductance.
outline: First law: changing flux linkage induces an EMF; second law: e = −N dΦ/dt
Lenz's law fixes the minus sign
L = NΦ/I and e = −L di/dt; M = N₂Φ₂₁/I₁ and e₂ = −M di₁/dt
Coefficient of coupling k = M/√(L₁L₂), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1

bank.q: Describe the construction of a single-phase transformer with a neat sketch. Explain its working and prove that V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁.
outline: Core type and shell type; laminated silicon steel; two windings insulated from each other and from the core
Primary draws alternating current, sets up alternating mutual flux in the core
Same flux links both windings, so induced EMF per turn is the same: E₁/N₁ = E₂/N₂
Ideal transformer: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ = I₁/I₂, with step-up and step-down cases
No moving parts; state why rating is in kVA

bank.q: Explain the construction and working principle of a DC machine. Show how the same machine works as a generator and as a motor, and explain the role of the commutator.
outline: Yoke, poles with field winding, armature with commutator, brushes
Generator: prime mover rotates armature in field, coil EMF e = B l v, commutator rectifies to DC; E = PΦNZ/60A
Motor: DC in armature interacts with field flux to give torque T ∝ ΦI_a; commutator reverses current every half turn
Back EMF E_b = V − I_aR_a limits armature current
Same machine, direction of power flow decides the name

bank.q: Explain how a rotating magnetic field is produced in a three-phase induction motor. Define synchronous speed and slip, and describe the torque–slip characteristic.
outline: Three windings 120° apart carry three-phase currents; resultant field of constant magnitude rotates at N_s
N_s = 120f/P with f in Hz
Rotor cuts the field, induced currents give torque; rotor must run below N_s
s = (N_s − N)/N_s; rotor frequency = s f
Torque rises to pull-out value at s_max = R₂/X₂ then falls; starting torque is low, normal running slip is a few percent

bank.q: An iron ring of mean length 50 cm and cross-section 4 cm² carries a coil of 400 turns with 2 A. Take μᵣ = 1000. Find the flux. Repeat with a 1 mm air gap in the ring and comment on the result.
outline: F = NI = 800 A·t
S_iron = l/(μ₀μᵣA); compute and get flux with Φ = F/S
Add S_gap = l_g/(μ₀A) in series for the gapped case
Show flux falls steeply even though the gap is short
Comment: gap reluctance dominates; that is why machine gaps are kept small
State assumption: no fringing, no saturation

bank.q: A single-phase transformer has 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns, with 230 V applied to the primary. Find the secondary voltage and the primary current when the secondary supplies 20 A. State the assumptions used.
outline: Ideal transformer: V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ gives I₁ = 4 A
Assumptions: ideal core, no leakage, no losses, unity coupling
Mention magnetising current makes the real primary current slightly larger

bank.q: Two coils of 200 and 400 turns share a core. A current changing at 50 A/s in coil 1 induces 20 V in coil 2. Find the mutual inductance. If L₁ = 0.4 H and L₂ = 0.9 H, find the coefficient of coupling.
outline: e₂ = M di₁/dt gives M = 20/50 = 0.4 H
Interpret: about two-thirds of the flux links both coils, the rest is leakage

bank.q: A 4-pole, 50 Hz three-phase induction motor runs at 1440 r/min at full load. Find the synchronous speed, the slip and the rotor frequency. Also state the speed at which pull-out torque occurs if R₂ = 0.2 Ω per phase and standstill reactance X₂ = 1 Ω per phase.
outline: N_s = 120f/P = 1500 r/min
Rotor frequency = s f = 2 Hz

bank.q: A 220 V DC shunt motor has an armature resistance of 0.5 Ω and takes an armature current of 20 A. Calculate the back EMF. Explain what happens to the speed if the field flux is halved while the load torque stays constant.
outline: T ∝ ΦI_a; halving flux needs double armature current for the same torque
E_b ∝ ΦN, so speed must roughly double if E_b is unchanged; in practice E_b falls slightly because of the larger I_aR_a drop
Warn that this is why field failure races a DC motor

bank.q: Compare a three-phase induction motor with a synchronous motor on starting, speed, power factor and application. Explain why the synchronous motor cannot start on its own.
outline: Induction motor: self-starting, slip, lagging power factor, rugged
Synchronous: runs exactly at N_s, needs DC excitation, can supply leading VARs
At standstill the rotating field sweeps past the rotor too fast; average torque over a cycle is zero, so the rotor never locks
Starting aids: damper winding, pony motor, VFD at low frequency
Application split: pumps, fans and conveyors versus large compressors and power-factor correction

bank.q: Using double revolving field theory, explain why a single-phase induction motor produces no starting torque. Describe two starting methods and their trade-offs.
outline: Pulsating field = two equal fields rotating opposite ways at N_s
At standstill the two give equal and opposite torques; once spun, the forward field dominates
Split-phase: resistance-divided start winding, cheap, low starting torque, needs a centrifugal switch
Capacitor-start and capacitor-run; shaded pole for small fans
Universal motor as an alternative where AC/DC both needed

bank.q: A pick-and-place machine needs three drives: a precise positioner, an accurate rotary table and an energy-efficient continuous fan drive. Choose among stepper, servo, BLDC and single-phase induction motors, and justify each choice.
outline: Positioner: stepper or servo; stepper is open-loop and cheap, servo is closed-loop and holds position under load
Rotary table needing accuracy under varying load: servo with encoder feedback
Continuous fan: BLDC for efficiency and speed control, or induction motor where cost matters and speed is fixed
Compare on torque, cost, control complexity, maintenance and efficiency

bank.q: A small factory has a lagging power factor and pays a penalty. Discuss how a synchronous motor could help, what starting method you would use, and what the limits of this solution are.
outline: Over-excited synchronous motor draws leading current and supplies reactive power, raising plant power factor
Sizing the motor near the VAR deficit; it runs at fixed speed only
Cannot self-start: damper winding or reduced-voltage/VFD start; synchronising procedure after run-up
Limits: cost, maintenance of DC excitation and slip rings, risk of losing synchronism on overload

glossary.def: The total magnetic field passing through an area, measured in weber (Wb), symbol Φ.
Flux per unit area, B = Φ/A, measured in tesla (T).
The opposition a magnetic path offers to flux, S = l/(μ₀μᵣA), in A/Wb.
A material's ability to carry flux; μ = μ₀μᵣ, with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m for free space.
The state where extra MMF barely increases flux because the iron's domains are all aligned.
Flux that links one coil but not the other, so it does useful work in neither.
The induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of flux linkage through it.
The induced EMF drives a current whose own field opposes the change that produced it.
Flux linkage per ampere in the same coil, L = NΦ/I, measured in henry (H).
Flux linkage in one coil per ampere of current in another, M, also in henry.
The fraction of flux shared by two coils, k = M/√(L₁L₂), from 0 to 1.
Circulating current induced inside a solid iron core by changing flux; it heats the core and is cut by lamination.
Energy lost per cycle as the core is magnetised back and forth; reduced by using silicon steel.
A static device with two windings on one core that changes AC voltage level at nearly constant power.
The ratio of primary to secondary turns, which also equals the voltage ratio of an ideal transformer.
The EMF generated by a motor's own armature rotation, which opposes the supply and sets the current drawn.
A segmented cylinder with carbon brushes that reverses armature coil connections at the right instant.
The speed of the rotating magnetic field, N_s = 120f/P, fixed by supply frequency and pole count.
The fractional shortfall of rotor speed below synchronous speed, s = (N_s − N)/N_s.
Bars shorted by end rings, with no external circuit; simple and rugged but slip cannot be added externally.
The DC current fed to a field winding, which sets the flux and hence the internal EMF of a machine.
The fixed shaft rotation produced by one pulse of a stepper drive, 360° divided by steps per revolution.
A motor packaged with a position or speed sensor and driven in closed loop so the shaft follows a command.
A permanent-magnet rotor motor whose stator currents are switched electronically, so no brushes or commutator are needed.
